subject: system-design
title: The RESHADED Framework
summary: A repeatable eight-step structure that turns any open-ended system-design interview into a checklist you can work through under pressure.

blocks.text: A system-design interview is open-ended on purpose, and that's what makes it stressful — there's no single right answer and no obvious place to start. A framework fixes that: instead of inventing a path each time, you walk the same steps in the same order, so your time goes to the design and not to deciding what to do next. RESHADED is one such structure.

items: Requirements — the functional features and the non-functional targets (availability, latency, scale).
Estimation — back-of-the-envelope numbers for traffic, storage, and bandwidth.
Storage schema — the data model: entities, fields, and how they relate.
High-level design — the major components and how a request flows between them.
API design — the key endpoints that expose the features.
Detailed design — scaling each component and removing bottlenecks.
Evaluation — checking the design back against the requirements.
Distinctive features — the extras that fit this particular problem.

blocks.text: Requirements and Estimation come first because everything downstream depends on them. The features decide which components you need; the numbers decide how big each one has to be. A design for a thousand users and one for a billion are different systems, so pin the scale before you commit to any structure.

blocks.title: Don't draw boxes too early
blocks.text: Never start sketching components before you've nailed the requirements and rough scale. A clean diagram that solves the wrong problem — or the wrong size of problem — wins no points.

With requirements and numbers in hand, lay out the data model and a high-level design that satisfies the features end to end. Only then go deep: in Detailed design you scale each piece — add a cache, partition the database, put work behind a queue — and call out where the bottlenecks would appear under your estimated load.

Evaluation is the step candidates skip, and it's where you show seniority. Walk the design back against each non-functional target and name the tradeoffs you made. Distinctive features then let you tailor the answer to the specific prompt — a news feed's ranking, a chat app's delivery guarantees, a video site's CDN.

blocks.title: A rough time budget
blocks.text: In a 45-minute round, spend the first 10 or so on requirements and estimation, the middle stretch on high-level and detailed design, and leave a few minutes at the end to evaluate. Front-loading the requirements is what keeps the rest on track.
The point of RESHADED isn't to recite eight words — it's to never freeze. When the prompt is vague and the whiteboard is blank, the framework gives you the next move, every time.
